CHAPTER 01  —  A NEW STORY BEGINS

Eleven
Fifty-Nine.

The night before everything changed.

11:59 p.m. · The ordinary worldThe city was having a perfectly ordinary night. Traffic. Rain. Someone insisting that one more episode didn't count as staying up late.
A very important notification
11:59 PM · TONIGHT
23:59
ONE MINUTE TO YOUR BIRTHDAY
And then ...
TICK.
There should have been a tock.
But the second hand didn't move. Neither did the traffic. Neither did the rain.
PANEL 03 · THE STILLNESS
The whole world was holding its breath.
OUR PROTAGONIST

Dhanu.

He had plans for his birthday. Saving the first minute of tomorrow was not one of them.

He reached for his phone.
11:59. Still.

Then came a sound that shouldn't have been possible.
KREE!
Something was moving.
From above the rooftops
A storm petrel.
A copper ring.
A letter.
Before you ask — yes, I can talk. The name’s Nix.
You’re a talking bird?!
“Interesting. The city has frozen and you're worried about the bird. This is going to be a long night.”
The petrel — who introduced himself as Nix — dropped the envelope into Dhanu’s hands. It was sealed with a strange symbol: a clock face without a minute hand.
✦ Unscheduled delivery · For Dhanu

A letter from tomorrow.

It was addressed to him, in handwriting that looked disturbingly familiar.

✉ Break the seal and read

To Dhanu,

If you're reading this, the first minute of your birthday is missing. Someone stole it. And if the minute doesn't return, tomorrow will never arrive.

There's a watch called Manifesto. It doesn't predict your future. It lets you choose what to do with the time you have.

Find the old harbour. Take the boat that has no flag. Whatever you do, don't follow the loudest road.

One last thing. When every clock stops, look for what still moves.

— You, one year from now.

P.S. The bird is irritating, but he knows the way. Don't tell him I said that.

The signature was Dhanu’s.
The date was one year in the future.

And Nix was already hopping away, offended at being mistaken for a pigeon.
PANEL 07 · THE OLD QUARTER
Three roads.
One way out.

The first obstacle.

A story choice · No timer

The three exits lead to the clock tower, the iron gate, and the old canal. Everything in the city has stopped. You only have the clue from the letter.

“When every clock stops, look for what still moves.”
Which path would you take?
Beyond the third archThe old canal was moving. Slowly. Silently. As if it hadn't heard that time was supposed to stop.
“Well done,” said Nix. “You've been promoted from luggage to passenger.”
They followed the water through an alley no map remembered. The sound of the city disappeared behind them. Then the fog opened.
PANEL 09 · THE FLAGLESS FERRY
A ship with no flag.
And someone waiting on deck.
The figure turned toward Dhanu.
Same posture. Same red scarf.

The same face.
The stranger smiled
“You're late.”
A pause
“I was, too.”
MANIFESTO / THE MISSING MINUTE
II

THE NEXT PART OF DHANU'S STORY

The Ship of
Forgotten Tomorrows.

Some voyages are measured in miles.
This one was measured in what you refuse to leave behind.

TURN THE PAGE ↓
THE FLAGLESS FERRY · 12:00 THAT NEVER CAMEDhanu stared at the stranger on deck. Same face. Same height. Even the old habit of putting one hand in his pocket when he didn’t know what to say.
PANEL 10 · THE OTHER PASSENGER
“You’re late,”
said his own voice.
DHANU“For what?”
THE STRANGER“For the first time you meet someone who knows how this ends.”
Dhanu took a step closer. The stranger took a step back. Their shadows did not move in the same direction.
PANEL 11 · AN IMPERFECT REFLECTION
“You’re me.”
“Almost.”
A VERY BAD EXPLANATION“A possible tomorrow,” the stranger said. “One of many. I boarded this ship a long time ago. I wanted to know every danger before I chose a direction.”
“And?” Dhanu asked.

“I’m still here.”
Nix landed on the ship’s rail. “Lovely reunion. Shall I put the two of you down as one passenger or two disappointments?”
A cold wind moved over the deck. The city behind them disappeared into fog. Ahead, a hundred ships floated without crews — some magnificent, some barely more than broken wood. Every one was perfectly still.
PANEL 12 · THE SEA OF ALMOSTS
A graveyard of journeys
that never began.
There were ships that never left because they waited for better weather. Others had turned back at the first storm. One had a perfectly polished hull and no sails at all.
“That one,” Nix said, nodding toward the polished ship, “spent twelve years picking a name.”
The stranger unrolled a map. It was blank except for three tiny ink marks. “Manifesto lies beyond this sea. When the storm comes, follow the brightest beacon. It always looks safe.”
Dhanu noticed the word looks. The stranger noticed him noticing.
THE WIND DIED.THEN THE SEA STOOD UP.
PANEL 13 · THE HOURLESS STORM
Three beacons.
One way through.
A wave tore across the deck. Dhanu grabbed the railing. The stranger had already retreated below, clutching the useless map.
“Good news,” Nix shouted over the wind. “This is a very educational way to drown.”
Then a radio, rusted into the captain’s desk, crackled to life. That made no sense. There was no electricity. There was barely a tomorrow.
PANEL 14 · THE IMPOSSIBLE SIGNAL
A voice came through
the static.
INCOMING TRANSMISSION 00:00 / UNKNOWN

SANJAY: “Dhanu? I don't know where this is reaching you. Listen. Don't follow whatever is shouting the loudest.”

DHANU: “Sanjay?! How are you—”

SANJAY: “Bro, questions later. You need an answer? First make sure something can answer back.”

— SIGNAL LOST —

Dhanu tried the dial again. Nothing. The signal had lasted only a few seconds, but it was enough to make the whole impossible ocean feel a little less empty.
Nix tapped the ship’s bell with his beak. “Your friend is annoyingly sensible. Shall we see which light can hear us?”
OBSTACLE TWO · THE BEACON TEST

Don't follow the light.
Find the one that answers.

The storm has swallowed the chart. Three beacons are visible. One flashes endlessly, one only reflects lightning, and one is tended by someone who can hear the ship. Ring the bell, watch what happens, then choose your route.

01 · RED LANTERN
02 · SILVER MIRROR
03 · GREEN LIGHT

The lights are too far away to identify. Try making a sound.

THE GREEN BEACON · BEYOND THE REEFThe green lantern went dark once, then twice. Not a loop. Not a reflection. An answer. Dhanu turned the wheel toward it as the wave behind them broke.
“You were right,” Nix said.

“Sanjay was right,” Dhanu replied.

“Don’t ruin this for me.”
The ferry slipped between two reefs with barely a hand’s width to spare. The storm folded shut behind them like a door.
Only then did Dhanu realise the stranger was still standing at the far end of the deck — dry, motionless, untouched by the rain.
DHANU“Why didn’t you help?”
THE STRANGER“Because the last time I chose, I lost something I couldn’t bring back.”
The stranger reached out. For one second his hand went straight through the railing. A thousand pale fragments stirred where his fingers should have been.
“I'm not the Dhanu who will exist,” he said, almost too quietly to hear. “I am one possible Dhanu who never left this ship. Manifesto kept the choice. The sea kept me.”
“Then come with us.”

“I can't. But you can stop another ship from ending up here.”
He pressed a small brass gear into Dhanu’s palm. It was warm. A single word had been engraved along its edge:
✺
THE FIRST FRAGMENT OF MANIFESTOBEGIN.
When Dhanu looked up, the stranger was gone. His reflection remained on the wet deck for a heartbeat longer, then vanished too.
Ahead, an island climbed out of the mist. A narrow staircase wound toward a temple perched above the clouds. There were no lights. No flags. Only the dull thud of a wooden striker, striking something that refused to ring.
PANEL 15 · THE NEXT SHORE
At the top of the mountain,
someone was still training.
Dhanu checked the letter from tomorrow.
Under the original warning, a new line had appeared.
THE INK WAS STILL WET

“The first journey takes courage.
The next one takes every morning.”

THE END OF CHAPTER TWO

The next step
is the hard one.

A mountain. An impossible training ritual. And the one thing no legendary watch can give him for free.

III

A STORY ABOUT SHOWING UP AGAIN

The Thousandth
Morning.

The mountain didn't ask Dhanu to be extraordinary.
It asked him to come back.

ASCEND THE MOUNTAIN ↓
THE FIRST LIGHT / THE ISLAND ABOVE THE CLOUDSBy the time Dhanu reached the staircase, the sea had vanished under a sheet of mist. The steps were narrow, uneven, and carved into the mountain itself. Beside the first one, someone had written a number: ONE.
PANEL 16 · A STAIRCASE WITHOUT AN END
The stairs climbed into
an unfinished morning.
The next step said TWO. Then THREE. Then FOUR. Somewhere above the mist, pale sunlight reached the mountain, though midnight had never arrived below. Dhanu looked up. There were far too many steps to count.
“How high is this temple?” Dhanu asked.

“Depends,” said Nix. “How good are you at regretting your decisions?”
Halfway up, he found another number painted into the stone: 999. Beyond it, a landing. An open gate. And a courtyard worn smooth by the same pair of feet moving along the same line.
PANEL 17 · THE COURTYARD
A thousand paths,
worn into one.
An old bellkeeper stood in the courtyard, practising with a plain wooden staff. Step. Turn. Strike. Return. No flourish. No audience. Each movement ended exactly where the next one began.
DHANU“Are you training for something?”
THE BELLKEEPER“I was. Then I realised I was training for every day after that.”
The bellkeeper lowered the staff. His hands were rough. His sleeves had been repaired so often that almost none of the original cloth remained. Behind him hung an enormous bronze bell.
There were 999 tally marks cut into the wall. The last was fresh.
PANEL 18 · THE SILENT BELL
Nine hundred and ninety-nine strikes.
Not one sound.
“That bell has been silent for 999 mornings,” the bellkeeper said. “The second piece of Manifesto rests inside it. Ring it, and it's yours.”
“That's it?”

“That's everything.”
Dhanu took the wooden striker. He swung. The bronze shuddered. No note followed — only a dull thud. He swung harder. A second thud. Nix winced.
THUD....THUD.
“You can keep striking,” said the bellkeeper. “Or you can tell me what changed between the first and the second.”
Dhanu examined the bell. A thick iron brace was pressed against its side. Above it hung a counterweight, pulled just slightly out of line. Someone had been trying to ring a bell that could barely move.
“Did you know it was jammed?” Dhanu asked.

The bellkeeper looked at his own 999 marks.

“I needed a thousand mornings to learn to look properly.”
For a moment neither spoke. Then the old man handed the striker back. This time he stepped aside.
OBSTACLE THREE · THE SILENT BELL

The next attempt
must be different.

Dhanu knows why the bell failed. Decide what he should do before swinging again. No timer, no penalty, and the story can always continue.

The bell is held still by the brace. How should Dhanu approach his next attempt?

THE THOUSANDTH ATTEMPTDhanu knelt beside the bell. He loosened the iron brace. He shifted the counterweight until the bell hung true. Then he stepped back and raised the wooden striker.
He had not grown stronger in those few minutes. He had simply stopped making the same mistake.
D O O O O N G
PANEL 19 · ONE SOUND, AT LAST
The mountain answered.
So did the minute.
The sound crossed the courtyard, the steps, the sea. Far below, a wave struck the shore. For the first time since 11:59, a frozen cloud moved. Dhanu's phone flickered.
LOCKED CLOCK11:59:59The final second has returned. Not the minute.
The bellkeeper opened the little door beneath the bronze shell. Inside rested a second brass gear, smaller than the first. Its teeth caught the dawn like sparks.
✺
THE SECOND FRAGMENT OF MANIFESTORETURN.
DHANU“So the first 999 mornings weren't wasted?”
THE BELLKEEPER“Some were. I wasted them by refusing to learn. You didn't.”
As Dhanu placed the gears together, they turned once in his palm. The letter from tomorrow grew warm. Its wax seal cracked a second time — without anyone touching it.
On the back of the letter, beneath a smear of old ink, another line slowly came into view. It wasn't in the same handwriting as the rest.
A MESSAGE HIDDEN UNDER THE SEAL

“The minute was never stolen.
It was promised.”

Dhanu looked toward the horizon.

Beyond the mountains, a city had appeared where there had been nothing before — sealed behind a wall so enormous it cut through the clouds.
PANEL 20 · THE NEXT DESTINATION
A city behind a wall.
And a promise he never made.
“Nix?” Dhanu said.

“Yes?”

“Tell me that letter is lying.”

For once, the bird had no joke.
THE END OF CHAPTER THREE

Some promises
have a price.

Beyond the wall is a city that remembers things Dhanu hasn't lived. And someone is waiting to collect what he supposedly owes.

IV

THE CITY OF RECORDS AND KEPT PROMISES

The City
Behind the Wall.

In Vesper, every hour has a record.
But one minute has been filed under Dhanu’s name.

ENTER VESPER ↓
THE EDGE OF VESPER · 11:59:59 The wall rose beyond the mountain like a second horizon. It cut the clouds in half. A hundred watchtowers crowned its upper edge. None of them had guards.
There was, however, a queue. Nobody in it moved. Their faces were turned toward an enormous gate, and every wrist held a watch with its hands missing.
Dhanu stopped in front of the gate. Above it, four words had been pressed into dark bronze:
EVERY PROMISE HAS A WITNESS.
DHANU“Why does this place feel like it's waiting for me?”
NIX“Because the gate has just started breathing.”
The bronze doors opened by an inch. A voice rolled out of the gap, dry as paper.
“Dhanu. The account holder has arrived.”
“Account holder?” Dhanu asked. “The letter says I owe someone a minute.”

“Then,” answered the voice, “you have been reading it from the wrong side.”
Inside lay a city without sunrise. Trams sat abandoned on their rails. Windows glowed in buildings where nobody lived. At every crossing, the clocks pointed in different directions—as though each was trying to remember a different yesterday.
Nix perched on a bent street sign. “On the bright side, we found a place where everyone is as punctual as you.”

“I am punctual.”

“You arrived at midnight yesterday.”
At the end of the street stood the Office of Unspent Tomorrows. A brass plaque on its door explained what the city did: Hours surrendered. Hours reserved. Hours returned.

For the first time that night, Dhanu understood that a frozen minute might not be a punishment. It might be a transaction.
KLIKTHE DOOR UNLOCKED ITSELF
Behind a long wooden desk, an archivist was closing a ledger. Her hands were stained with blue ink. Her eyes never left the page.
THE ARCHIVIST“You are here to collect what was left for you.”
DHANU“I didn't ask anyone to leave me anything.”
The archivist pushed three objects across the desk: a transfer slip, a cracked receiver, and a page torn from the ledger.
“Then you should know what you are being offered,” she said. “Look at the evidence. Decide which name belongs on the other side of the promise.”
THE RECEIVER · A MESSAGE FROM OUTSIDE

“Dhanu? It's Siri.”

“I tried calling just before midnight. Somebody answered in your voice, but it wasn't you. He said, ‘He'll thank me when he stops making mistakes.’ Then the call cut out.”

“Whatever he promised, remember this: he doesn't get to decide for you.”

RECORDING ENDS · ORIGIN: 11:59 P.M.
Dhanu stared at the receiver. His chest tightened for a second. Then he turned it over. The battery compartment was empty. There was no signal. Yet her voice had reached him.

It wasn't magic, he realised. It was evidence.
OBSTACLE FOUR · THE PROMISE LEDGER

Read the record.
Not the rumour.

Three exhibits. One contradiction. Examine the records, then decide whose name the missing minute was meant for.

Choose an exhibit to read its original record. Three things were left on the desk for a reason.

According to the contract, Dhanu is the…

Read the evidence before deciding.

THE NAME IN THE SECOND COLUMN He read the slip again. BENEFICIARY: DHANU. The words did not move. The ink did not change. He had spent the night chasing a thief when, in the city's records, he was the person waiting to receive something.
“If I'm the one it's for,” Dhanu said, “then who put it here?”
The archivist finally looked up. “Someone with your face. Someone so afraid of the years ahead that he tried to save them before they happened.”
Dhanu thought of the ship crowded with voyages nobody had begun. The bellkeeper repeating the same failed strike. The stranger who had stepped backward when Dhanu stepped forward.

There was a pattern. He had been looking at the three places as separate tests. They were parts of the same question.
THE GATE WAS NOT LOCKING HIM OUT.IT WAS KEEPING SOMETHING IN.
The archivist opened a small compartment in the desk. Inside rested the third mechanism of Manifesto: a gear with a thin band of glass running around its edge. There was a single word cut into the metal.
✺THIRD FRAGMENT OF MANIFESTOWITNESS.

Some truths need another person to be heard.

The third gear touched the first two. BEGIN. RETURN. WITNESS.

Their teeth caught, then stopped. There should have been a fourth piece. Instead, a narrow line of red light appeared in the wall behind the archivist.
Beyond the wall, a man stood in the turning shadows. Same height. Same face. Same impossible familiarity.

The stranger from the ship had beaten him there. His wrist caught the light for an instant: a fourth golden mechanism was fastened over his watch.
THE OTHER DHANU“I kept it safe. I kept you safe.”
DHANU“You kept me from choosing.”
For once, there was no answer. Only the faint sound of a watch beginning to tick backward.
THE FINAL WARNING

“The last piece of Manifesto
cannot be taken.
It must be given.”

THE END OF CHAPTER FOUR

The hour
you choose.

Dhanu has the first three pieces. The fourth is strapped to the wrist of the life he might have lived. And that life will not let go.

V

FINAL ARC · THE CHOICE THAT MOVES TIME

The Hour
You Choose.

One locked minute. Two possible lives.
And a choice no one can make for Dhanu.

ENTER THE FINAL ARC ↓

High above Vesper, where the old meridian line crossed the city’s clocks, Dhanu found the vault of Manifesto. It was not a treasure room in the ordinary sense. It was an observatory of kept hours — a place where one chosen minute could be held away from the world.

The man waiting beside the mechanism wore Dhanu’s face, only older, weathered, and tired in a way that came not from battle but from hesitation. He admitted what the record had only implied: when he once stood at the edge of his own next life, he had hidden a minute inside Manifesto so he would not have to step forward before he was ready.

That was the cost of the Sea of Almosts. The minute stayed safe, but the life around it grew smaller. Legends had chased Manifesto for years — sailors, swordsmen, scouts, city-watchers — but the watch was never meant to give a future. It only asked one question: when your next arc arrives, will you live it, or will you hide from it?

OBSTACLE FIVE · THE LAST DECISION

What should Dhanu do
with the missing minute?

The older Dhanu placed his hand over Manifesto. Its gears trembled at 11:59. Three paths opened in the turning brass. The minute was his to live. But the final gear was still in the other Dhanu’s hand. What would he ask for?

Read the confrontation, then decide how Dhanu should answer the watch.

Manifesto’s last secret. The watch had never stolen tomorrow. It had guarded one minute for a man who feared choosing what came next. Dhanu held out his hand. The older Dhanu, afraid and uncertain, gave him the last gear freely. No villain fell. No future was erased. With BEGIN, RETURN, WITNESS and CHOOSE joined at last, Dhanu returned the promised minute to the world. He could not know every road ahead — but he could take the first step.
For Dhanu — from your people. Happy Birthday, bro. May the days ahead bring good adventures, the discipline to build what matters, and people worth coming home to. And as graduation draws closer, may your next chapter be one you’re excited to write.
